guide.title: Child Abuse & Neglect
guide.lead: You may be the only professional who sees inside the home. Look for injuries that don't fit the story or the child's development, treat the child, write down exactly what you see and hear, and report your concern. You don't need proof: reasonable suspicion is enough.

sections.title: Red flags in the story
items: No explanation, or one that changes
The mechanism doesn't fit the child's development ("he rolled off the couch" at 2 weeks)
Delay in seeking care
Blaming a sibling or the child
Caregiver hostile, indifferent or unwilling to leave
Many previous visits for injuries

groups.title: TEN-4
items: Torso, Ears or Neck in a child under 4 years
Any bruise in a baby 4 months or younger

groups.title: FACESp
items: Frenulum (torn)
Angle of the jaw
Cheeks (fleshy part)
Eyelids
Subconjunctival bleeding
patterned bruises (hand, loop, belt, bite)

sections.title: Injuries that suggest abuse
rows: On protected areas (TEN-4-FACESp), patterned, clustered, or in a baby who can't cruise. Don't try to date bruises by colour.
Immersion with sharp lines (stocking or glove pattern), spared skin creases or buttock centre, small round cigarette-sized burns, object shapes (iron, grill).
Posterior ribs, metaphyseal corner fractures, femur or humerus in a child who can't walk, several fractures of different ages.
Abusive head trauma: vomiting, irritability, lethargy, seizures, apnoea, bulging fontanelle – often without marks. Most common under 1 year.
Bruising, vomiting or shock with no clear story.

steps.title: Treat
steps.text: ABCs and a full exam, with a second person present. Keep the child warm and covered.

steps.title: Listen, don't interview
steps.text: Open questions only ("Tell me what happened"). Write the child's and caregiver's exact words.

steps.title: Don't confront
steps.text: No accusations. Explain that the injuries need hospital care.

steps.title: Document
steps.text: Objective findings and a body map, each explanation word for word, the home's condition, times.

steps.title: Report
steps.text: To child protection or police according to local law, and tell the receiving clinician. Reports made in good faith are protected in most countries.

steps.title: Keep the child safe
steps.text: If the child is in immediate danger, don't leave them there; call police.

groups.title: Neglect
items: Failure to thrive, hunger, hoarding food
Poor hygiene, wrong clothing for the weather
Untreated illness or dental problems, missed immunizations
Left unsupervised; unsafe home

groups.title: Fabricated or induced illness
items: Symptoms only ever seen by the caregiver
Many hospitals and tests, no cause found
Caregiver unusually knowledgeable and keen on procedures

sections.title: Sudden unexpected infant death
items: Record position, bedding, room temperature, who found the baby and when
Leave bedding and objects in place; don't wash the baby
Support the family; avoid blame
Safe sleep: on the back, own flat cot, no soft bedding or pillows

quiz.q: 6-month-old, irritable and vomiting, 'rolled off the couch'. No marks, lethargic, bulging fontanelle. Suspect:
quiz.explanation: Head injury without marks is common in abusive head trauma; meningitis is the other must-not-miss.

quiz.q: To report suspected child abuse you need:
quiz.explanation: Reports in good faith are protected in most countries.

quiz.q: 3-year-old with many bruises, including a handprint on the face; 'falls a lot'. Best action?
options: Document objectively, transport, and report your concern
quiz.explanation: A handprint on the cheek is a patterned bruise in a protected area.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a sign of neglect?
options: A clean child dressed for the weather
quiz.explanation: The others are classic neglect signs.

quiz.q: Burns on both feet with a sharp line above the ankles and even depth; 'stepped in the bath'. This suggests:
quiz.explanation: Accidental scalds are irregular with splash marks.

quiz.q: Many admissions for 'seizures' and 'allergies' only when the mother is present; no cause found despite many specialists. Consider:
options: Fabricated or induced illness (medical child abuse)
quiz.explanation: Also called factitious disorder imposed on another.

quiz.q: The father of a child with suspected abuse keeps asking if you'll call the police and becomes agitated. You:
options: Stay calm, say you follow the law, keep him away from the patient area, call police if safety is at risk
quiz.explanation: Your and the child's safety come first.

quiz.q: A bruise on the ear of a 2-year-old:
options: Should be dated by its colour
quiz.explanation: Torso, ears and neck bruising under 4 years suggests abuse.

quiz.q: Dating bruises by their colour is:
options: Unreliable: describe them, don't date them

quiz.q: Which fracture is most specific for abuse in infants?
options: Wrist buckle fracture after a fall
quiz.explanation: They come from squeezing the chest.

flashcards.question: Abusive head trauma: classic findings
flashcards.answer: Subdural bleeding, retinal haemorrhages and brain swelling. Signs: vomiting, irritability, lethargy, seizures, apnoea – often no external marks.

flashcards.question: Bruises suggesting abuse
flashcards.answer: TEN-4-FACESp: torso, ears, neck under 4 years; any bruise at 4 months or younger; frenulum, jaw angle, cheeks, eyelids, subconjunctival; patterned marks.

flashcards.question: Your legal duty
flashcards.answer: Report reasonable suspicion to child protection or police according to local law. No proof needed; good-faith reports are protected. Don't accuse; document objectively.

flashcards.question: Fractures suspicious for abuse
flashcards.answer: Posterior ribs, metaphyseal corner fractures, femur or humerus in a child who can't walk, multiple fractures of different ages.

flashcards.question: Fabricated or induced illness
flashcards.answer: A caregiver invents, exaggerates or causes illness in a child. Red flags: symptoms only when the caregiver is there, many hospitals and tests, no cause found.

flashcards.question: Documenting suspected abuse
flashcards.answer: Describe, don't diagnose. Exact words in quotes, each explanation, body map, scene, who you reported to and when.

flashcards.question: Signs of neglect
flashcards.answer: Failure to thrive, poor hygiene, wrong clothing, untreated illness, missed immunizations, no supervision, unsafe home, hunger.

flashcards.question: Burns suggesting abuse
flashcards.answer: Immersion with sharp lines (stocking or glove), spared skin creases, small round cigarette-sized burns, object-shaped burns. Accidental scalds are irregular with splashes.

critical.scenario: 4-month-old with the mother's boyfriend: 'won't stop crying', vomiting, lethargic, weak cry, bulging fontanelle, no bruises. His story changes to 'I had to shake him a little'. He wants to wait for the mother.
critical.question: Your priority?

options.t: Suspected abusive head trauma: transport now, involve police (he admitted shaking), record his exact words, don't leave the baby with him

options.f: The baby has a life-threatening head injury.
Lethargy and a bulging fontanelle need hospital now.

options.t: Ask child protection for permission to transport
options.f: Treat and transport first; report en route.

critical.explanation: Monitor the airway; seizures and apnoea are common.
critical.kpi: Recognizes abusive head trauma and ensures transport and reporting

critical.scenario: 6-year-old 'burned his hand playing with matches'. Round, deep, uniform burns on the palm and three more on the forearm, some fresh and some healed. He's quiet and avoids eye contact.
critical.question: Interpretation and plan?

options.t: Cigarette-type burns of different ages that don't fit the story: treat the burns, transport, document objectively, report; don't confront

options.f: Matches don't cause several uniform round burns of different ages.

options.t: Insist the child explains before you decide

critical.explanation: Patterned burns of different ages are a strong abuse indicator.
critical.kpi: Identifies patterned burn injuries inconsistent with history

critical.scenario: 7-year-old with a deformed forearm 'from gym class'. The school nurse documents a black eye and facial bruises in the past months, hunger, the same clothes, many missed days. The child is withdrawn and flinches.
critical.question: Your obligation?

options.t: Treat and transport; report suspected abuse and neglect; document each injury, the child's words and the school's records
Treat the fracture only; social issues aren't your role
options.f: You are often a mandated reporter.

options.t: Call the parents to explain first
options.f: That can put the child at risk.
Each professional reports their own concern.

critical.explanation: A pattern over time is more telling than any single injury.
critical.kpi: Fulfils reporting duties when abuse and neglect indicators coexist
